column2: And whatever trait of character a man has ... even if he thinks it hidden from people, it becomes known

Their dynasty continued for some 270 years, and they ruled the Station of Abraham, peace be upon him, and his place of prayer, the homeland of the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, and his burial place, the place where the pilgrims stand and where the angels descend. Then their rule came to an end. Throughout all this their partisans remained in the fullest measure of the obedience to them and love for them that they had always shown, and of belief in their lineage from the imam Ismāʿīl ibn Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq. Even after the dynasty was gone and its traces effaced, they rose up repeatedly, calling people to their innovation and proclaiming the names of boys from among their descendants, claiming that they were entitled to the caliphate and holding that they had been designated by bequest from the imams who preceded them. Had they doubted their lineage, they would not have braved perils in championing them. For a man of innovation does not obscure his affair, does not make his innovation ambiguous, and does not give the lie to himself in what he claims.

What is astonishing is the judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, the master of the speculative thinkers among the theologians: how he leans toward this weaker view and holds this feeble opinion! If it was because of the heresy in religion that they were given to and their deep involvement in Rāfiḍism, that does not repel their mission, nor does establishing their lineage avail them anything against God in their unbelief. For God the Exalted said to Noah, peace be upon him, concerning his son: “He is not of your family; his conduct is not righteous. So do not ask for what you have no knowledge of” (11: 46). And the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said to Fāṭima, admonishing her: “Fāṭima, act, for I shall not avail you anything against God.” And whenever a man knows a matter or is certain of a thing, he is bound to proclaim it openly; God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way. And these people were exposed to the suspicions of the dynasties about them and lived under the watch of tyrants, because their partisans were numerous and spread through the remote lands with their mission, and because their risings recurred time after time; so their leading men took refuge in concealment and were hardly known, as has been said:
If you were to ask the days what my name is, they would not know ... and where my place is, they would not recognize my place

So much so that Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl the imam, an ancestor of ʿUbayd Allāh al-Mahdī, was called “the Concealed” (al-Maktūm); his partisans gave him that name because they had agreed to keep him hidden, for fear of those who had overpowered them. The partisans of the Abbasids used this, when the ʿUbaydids appeared, as a means of attacking their lineage, and they drew near with this opinion, which speaks to the weak among their caliphs; and their supporters were delighted with it, as were the emirs of their dynasty who were in charge of their wars with the enemies, using it to ward off from themselves and their sultan the shame of being unable to resist and defend against those who had overcome them in Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz — the Kutāma Berbers, the partisans of the ʿUbaydids and the people of their mission. So much so that the judges in Baghdad entered a formal record denying them this lineage, and a group of eminent people testified to this before them, among them al-Sharīf al-Raḍī and his brother al-Murtaḍā and Ibn al-Baṭḥāwī, and of the scholars Abū Ḥāmid al-Isfarāyīnī, al-Qudūrī, al-Ṣaymarī, Ibn al-Akfānī, al-Abīwardī and Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Nuʿmān, the jurist of the Shīʿa, and others of the leading men of the community in Baghdad, on a notable day, in the year 460, in the days of al-Qādir. Their testimony in this rested on hearsay, on what had become widely known and recognized among the people in Baghdad, most of which consists of partisans of the Abbasids, who impugn this lineage. So the transmitters of reports passed it on as they had heard it and related it as they had retained it, and the truth lies behind it.

And in al-Muʿtaḍid’s letter concerning ʿUbayd Allāh, addressed to Ibn al-Aghlab in Qayrawān and Ibn Midrār in Sijilmāsa, there is the most truthful witness and the clearest proof of the soundness of their lineage; for al-Muʿtaḍid was better placed than anyone with regard to the lineage of the Prophet’s family. The dynasty and sovereignty are a market for the world: the wares of the sciences and crafts are brought to it, strayed pieces of wisdom are sought in it, the mounts of narrations and reports are driven toward it, and whatever sells there sells among everyone. If the dynasty keeps clear of arbitrariness, partiality, folly and pettiness, takes the straight path and does not stray from the right course, then pure gold and refined silver sell in its market; but if it goes along with private aims and grudges, and wrongdoing and falsehood surge among the brokers of the Arabs, then base coin and counterfeit sell. And the discerning critic is the scale of his own scrutiny, the balance of his inquiry and what he seeks.

The like of this, and what is much further from the truth, is often whispered by those who impugn the lineage of Idrīs ibn Idrīs ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God be pleased with them), the imam after his father in the far Maghrib. They hint, with an insinuation that incurs the legal penalty (ḥadd), at suspicion about the unborn child left behind by Idrīs the Elder, saying that he is Rāshid’s, their client. May God disgrace them and drive them far away! How ignorant they are! Do they not know that Idrīs the Elder — that he is Rāshid’s, their client. May God disgrace them and drive them far away! How great they are! Do they not know that Idrīs the Elder had his in-laws among the Berbers, and that from the time he entered the Maghrib until God, the Mighty and Majestic, took him he was deeply rooted in Bedouin life, and that the condition of the desert in such matters is no secret? They have no hiding places in which suspicion could arise, and the affairs of all their women are within sight of their women neighbors and within hearing of their neighbors, because the walls adjoin, the buildings are low and there are no partitions between the dwellings. Rāshid, after his master, was in charge of serving all the women of the household, in the presence of their supporters and partisans and under the observation of all of them. And the Berbers of the far Maghrib, all of them, agreed on pledging allegiance to Idrīs the Younger after his father, gave him their obedience willingly and by common consent, pledged themselves to him unto the red death, and plunged, in his defense, into seas of death in his wars and campaigns. Had they entertained such a doubt in themselves, or had it struck their ears, even from a malicious enemy or a doubting hypocrite, some of them at least would have held back from that. No, by God! These words came only from the Abbasids, their rivals, and from the Aghlabids, their agents, who were in Ifrīqiya, and their governors.

For when Idrīs the Elder fled to the Maghrib from the battle of Balkh, al-Hādī instructed the Aghlabids to lie in wait for him at the lookout posts and to set spies on him; but they did not catch him, and he made his way through to the Maghrib, where his affair was completed and his mission appeared. Afterward al-Rashīd learned what Wāḍiḥ, their client and their governor in Alexandria, had done by way of covert Shīʿite partisanship for the ʿAlids and his connivance in Idrīs’s escape to the Maghrib, and he killed him. Then he secretly sent in al-Shammākh, one of the clients of al-Mahdī, his father, to contrive the killing of Idrīs; he made a show of joining him and of disowning the Abbasids, his patrons, and Idrīs embraced him and drew him close to himself. In one of his private moments al-Shammākh handed him a poison by which he destroyed him. The news of his death fell upon the Abbasids most agreeably, for they hoped it would cut off the means of the ʿAlid mission in the Maghrib and tear out its stock. But when news reached them of the unborn child left behind by Idrīs, it took no longer than “No, no!” — and behold, the mission had returned, the Shīʿa in the Maghrib had come out into the open, and their dynasty had been renewed in Idrīs ibn Idrīs. That was more grievous to them than the strike of arrows. Weakness and senility had come upon the Arab dynasty, so that it could not aim at the far land; the limit of al-Rashīd’s power over Idrīs the Elder, in his place in the far Maghrib with the Berbers surrounding him, was only to contrive his destruction by poisons. So at that point they turned for help to their supporters, the Aghlabids in Ifrīqiya, to close that breach on their side, to cut off the disease that threatened the dynasty from their quarter, and to pull up those roots before they could take hold among them; al-Maʾmūn and the caliphs after him addressed them about this. But the Aghlabids were more helpless against the Berbers of the far Maghrib, and more in need of the like of it, a thrust against their own kings, because of what had befallen the caliphate: the non-Arab mamlūks had pounced upon its throne, mounted the saddle of mastery over it, and directed its commands at the will of their own aims in respect of its men, its revenues, the holders of its offices and all its undoing and binding, as their poet said:
A caliph in a cage ... between Waṣīf and Bughā / he says what they say to him ... as the parrot says

So these Aghlabid emirs, fearing the first outbursts of denunciations, resorted to excuses: sometimes by belittling the Maghrib and its people, sometimes by raising alarm about Idrīs, who had risen in it, and about those of his descendants who took his place, addressing them about his overstepping the borders of his district. And they sent his coinage along with their gifts and presents and the yield of their taxes, as a hint of his growing strength, an alarm at the strengthening of his might, a magnification of what they had been driven to in confronting and contending with him, and a threat to overturn the mission if they were forced to it. At other times they impugned Idrīs’s lineage with that same false slur, to lower his standing, not caring whether it was true or false, because of the distance and the feeble-mindedness of the Abbasid youths who came after and their non-Arab mamlūks, in accepting from any speaker and listening to every shouter. And this remained their habit until the Aghlabids’ rule came to an end. Then this hideous word struck the ears of the rabble, and some of the slanderers pricked up their ears at it and counted it a pretext for attacking their descendants when rivalry arose. What business have they, may God disgrace them, with turning away from the aims of the sharia, in which there is no conflict between what is certain and what is conjectured? Idrīs was born on his father’s bed, and the child belongs to the bed.

Moreover, to hold the Prophet’s family (ahl al-bayt) free of anything like this is among the beliefs of the people of faith: God, glory be to Him, has removed impurity from them and purified them thoroughly. So Idrīs’s bed is clean of defilement and free of impurity by the ruling of the Qurʾān, and whoever believes otherwise has incurred his own sin and entered unbelief by its door. I have gone on at length in this refutation only to close the doors of doubt and to repel the envier, because of what my own ears heard from the one who said it, who wrongs them and impugns their lineage with his fabrication, relating it, as he claims, from some historian of the Maghrib who deviated from the Prophet’s family and had doubts about believing in their forebears. Otherwise, the place is free of that and protected from it, and denying a fault where a fault is impossible is itself a fault. But I have pleaded for them in this present life, and I hope they will plead for me on the Day of Resurrection. And you should know that most of those who impugn their lineage are only those who envy the descendants of this Idrīs, whether one who claims to belong to the Prophet’s family or an intruder among them; for to claim this noble lineage is to claim a broad honor over the nations and generations of the people of all regions, and so suspicion arises about it.

And since the lineage of these descendants of Idrīs, in their homelands of Fez and the rest of the lands of the Maghrib, has reached such fame and clarity that it can scarcely be matched and no one hopes to attain it — for it is the transmission of a nation and generation of successors from a nation and generation of predecessors; the house of their ancestor Idrīs, the founder and builder of Fez, is among their houses; his mosque adjoins their quarter and their lanes; and his sword is unsheathed at the top of the great minaret in the center of their city, along with other traces of his, the reports of which have passed the bounds of widespread transmission (tawātur) several times over and almost amount to direct sight — when others of the people of this lineage look at what God has granted them of the like, and at what has reinforced their prophetic nobility in the majesty of the kingship that their forebears held in the Maghrib, and become certain that they stand apart from that and cannot reach a measure (mudd) of any one of them, nor half of it, and that the utmost for those who claim to belong to the noble House and have no such evidence is that their claim be conceded to them, since people are believed about their lineages — and there is a gulf between knowledge and conjecture, between certainty and concession — then when he knows this about himself he chokes on his spittle, and many of them wish they could turn them back from that honor to commoners and the base, out of envy from their own selves. So they resort to stubbornness, persist in obstinacy and slander with such a feeble slur and false statement, pleading equality in suspicion and similarity in the admission of possibility. How far from them is that! For, so far as we know, there is none in the Maghrib among the people of this noble House who attains, in the purity and clarity of his lineage, what the descendants of this Idrīs of the house of al-Ḥasan attain.

Their elders in the present age are the Banū ʿImrān in Fez, of the descendants of Yaḥyā al-Ḥawṭī ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā al-ʿAwwām ibn al-Qāsim ibn Idrīs ibn Idrīs. They are the chiefs (naqībs) of the Prophet’s family there and live in the house of their ancestor Idrīs, and they hold preeminence over all the people of the Maghrib, as we shall mention them when we come to the Idrisids, if God the Exalted wills. Akin to these corrupt statements and feeble doctrines is what the weak-minded among the jurists of the Maghrib take up in impugning the imam al-Mahdī, the founder of the Almohad dynasty, ascribing to him conjuring tricks and deception in what he undertook of upholding the true doctrine of God’s unity and in denouncing the oppressors who preceded him, and calling all his claims in this false — even in what the Almohads claim, in following him, concerning his affiliation to the Prophet’s family. What led the jurists to call him a liar was only the envy of his standing that lay hidden in their souls; for when they saw themselves as his match in knowledge and legal opinion and, as they claimed, in religion, and then he stood out from them in being followed in opinion, heeded in speech, and followed closely at the heels, they begrudged him that and belittled him by slandering his doctrines and calling his claims false. Furthermore, they were finding in the Lamtūna kings, his enemies, an esteem and honor that they found in no one else, because of the Lamtūna’s simplicity and their profession of religion; so the bearers of knowledge had, under their dynasty, a place of eminence and a seat in the councils of consultation, each in his own town

and according to his standing among his people. So they became partisans of them and at war with their enemy, and they resented the Mahdī for what he brought in opposing them, rebuking them and setting himself against them, out of partisanship for the Lamtūna and zeal for their dynasty, while the man’s standing was not theirs and his state was not in line with their beliefs. And what do you think of a man who resented in the people of the dynasty what he resented of their conditions, whose own independent legal reasoning differed from that of their jurists, who called out among his people and summoned them to fight them in person, who uprooted the dynasty from its foundations and turned it upside down when it was at its greatest in strength, sharpest in might and mightiest in supporters and defenders? Countless lives of his followers fell in this, known only to their Creator; they had pledged themselves to him unto death and shielded him from destruction with their own lives, and they drew near to God the Exalted by squandering their life-blood in making that mission manifest and in zeal for that word, until it rose above all words and the dynasties of the two shores gave way. And he was in a state of austerity, constraint, endurance of hardships and minimal use of this world until God took him, with no portion of enjoyment or possession in his worldly life, not even a child, to whom souls may incline while dissembling about their wish for one. So I wonder what he intended by that, if not the face of God, when no portion of this world came to him in this life. And besides, had his aim not been sound, his affair would not have been completed

and his mission spread wide — God’s way, which has already passed among His servants. As for their denial of his lineage among the Prophet’s family, no proof of theirs supports it; and besides, if it is established that he claimed it and attached himself to it, there is no evidence that can show it false, because people are believed about their lineages. And even if they say that leadership over a people is not exercised by anyone outside their own kind, which is correct, as will come in the first chapter of this book, the man led all the Maṣāmida, who submitted to following him and obeying him and his band from Hargha, until God’s command was fulfilled in his mission. Know, then, that the Mahdī’s affair did not depend on this Fāṭimī lineage, nor did people follow him because of it; they followed him only through the group solidarity (ʿaṣabiyya) of the Hargha and the Maṣmūda, his place within it and the firm rooting of his tree in it. That Fāṭimī lineage was hidden, effaced among the people, and it remained with him and with his clan, who passed it on among themselves; so the first lineage was as though he had shed it, put on the skin of these people and appeared in it, and the first affiliation does not harm him in his group solidarity, since it is unknown among the members of the band. The like of this often happens when the first lineage is hidden. Consider the story of ʿArfaja and Jarīr concerning the leadership of Bajīla, and how ʿArfaja was of the Azd

and put on the skin of Bajīla, until he disputed with Jarīr over leadership of them before ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, as is recorded; from it you will grasp the true aspect of the matter, and God is the guide to what is right. We have nearly strayed from the purpose of the book by dwelling at length on these errors; for the feet of many reliable authorities and retentive historians have slipped in such stories and opinions, and their minds have clung to them, and the general public, weak in insight and heedless of analogy, have passed them on from them; and they too received them in the same way, without investigation or reflection, and they were folded into their stores of memory, until the art of history became flimsy and confused, its student bewildered, and it came to be counted among the pursuits of the common people. The practitioner of this art therefore needs knowledge of the principles of statecraft, the natures of existing things, and the differences among nations, places and ages in ways of life, character, customs, creeds, schools of thought and all other conditions; a grasp of what is present of all this, and of the likeness between it and what is absent in their agreement, or the gulf between them in their disagreement; an explanation of what agrees and what differs among them; and a command of the foundations of dynasties and faiths, the beginnings of their appearance, the causes of their coming into being, the motives of their existence, and the conditions and reports of those who run them, until he has a full grasp of the causes of each report. Then he sets the transmitted report against the rules and principles he has: if it agrees with them and runs in accordance with what they require, it is sound; otherwise he rejects it as spurious and dispenses with it.

And the ancients held the science of history in high esteem only for this reason, so that al-Ṭabarī and al-Bukhārī, and Ibn Isḥāq before the two of them, and others like them among the scholars of the community took it up. Many have overlooked this secret in it, so that taking it up has become a mark of ignorance, and the common people, and those who have no firm footing in the branches of knowledge, think little of reading it, carrying it, plunging into it and intruding upon it; so the tended is mixed with the neglected, the kernel with the husk, and the truthful with the false; and to God belongs the outcome of all matters. Among the hidden errors in history is heedlessness of the change in conditions among nations and generations through the change of ages and the passing of days. It is a deep-seated disease, extremely hidden, for it occurs only after long stretches of time, so that hardly anyone notices it but a few individuals among the people of creation. The reason is that the conditions of the world and of nations, and their customs and creeds, do not continue in one uniform way and settled course; rather there is variation over days and eras and passing from one state to another. And as that happens with individuals, times and cities, so it happens in regions, territories, eras and dynasties — God’s way, which has already passed among His servants. There were in the world the nations of the first Persians, the Syriacs, the Nabateans, the Tubbaʿs, the Children of Israel and the Copts, and they had conditions peculiar to them in their dynasties and kingdoms, their governance, their crafts, languages and conventions, and all their common dealings with their own kind

and the conditions of their making the world flourish are attested by their remains. Then after them came the second Persians, the Rūm and the Arabs, and those conditions changed and customs were turned by them into what was of the same kind or similar, or into what differed or was remote from it. Then Islam came with the dynasty of Muḍar, and all those conditions turned again in another reversal and became what is mostly familiar in the present age, the later generations taking it from the earlier. Then the Arab dynasty and their days were effaced, the forebears who had built up their might and prepared the ground for their kingship passed away, and the matter passed into the hands of others, non-Arabs, such as the Turks in the East, the Berbers in the Maghrib and the Franks in the north. With their passing, nations went and conditions and customs were reversed whose story has been forgotten and whose matter has been neglected. The common cause of the change in conditions and customs is that the customs of every generation follow the customs of its sultan, as is said in the proverbs of wisdom, “People follow the religion of the king.” When the people of royal authority and sovereignty take over the dynasty and the government, they must resort to the customs of those before them and take many of them, without neglecting the customs of their own generation as well; so some difference arises in the dynasty’s customs from the customs of the first generation. And if another dynasty comes after them and mixes their customs with its own, it too differs somewhat, and more strongly from the first; and the gradation in difference continues until it ends in complete divergence. So as long as nations and generations succeed one another in royal authority and sovereignty, difference in customs and conditions never ceases to occur.

Analogy and imitation are a well-known nature in man, and are not safe from error; together with heedlessness and inattention they take him away from his purpose and bend him from his aim. A listener may hear many reports of those who have passed away and not notice the changes and reversals that have occurred in conditions, so that at first glance he applies them to what he knows and measures them by what he has seen, though the difference between them may be great, and he falls into a pit of error. Of this kind is what the historians relate of the circumstances of al-Ḥajjāj, that his father was one of the teachers, whereas in the present age teaching is one of the crafts of livelihood, far from the pride of the people of group solidarity, and the teacher is weak, wretched and cut off at the root. So many of the weak, people of trades and livelihood crafts, long to attain ranks for which they are not fit, and count them among the things possible for them; the whisperings of ambition carry them away, and sometimes its rope is cut from their hands and they fall into a pit of ruin and destruction, not knowing that it is impossible for them, that they are people of trades and crafts for livelihood, and that teaching in the early period of Islam and under the two dynasties was not like that. Knowledge in general was not a craft; it was only the transmission of what had been heard from the Lawgiver and the teaching of what was unknown of the religion, by way of delivering the message. So it was the people of lineages and group solidarity who upheld the faith who taught the Book of God and the sunna of His Prophet, God bless him

and grant him peace, in the sense of conveying information, not by way of instruction as a craft. For it was their Book, sent down upon the Messenger from among them, and in it was their guidance; Islam was their religion, for which they fought and were killed, and with which they were singled out from among the nations and honored. So they were eager to convey that and make the community understand it, not turned away from it by the reproach of arrogance nor restrained by the censure of pride. This is attested by the Prophet’s sending, God bless him and grant him peace, of his leading Companions with the delegations of the Arabs, to teach them the bounds of Islam and the laws of religion that he had brought; he sent for that purpose the ten of his Companions and those after them. No sooner had Islam been established and the roots of the faith intertwined than the distant nations took it from the hands of its people, its conditions changed with the passing of days, and the derivation of legal rulings from the texts increased because of the multiplicity and succession of cases. This required a canon to protect it from error, and knowledge became an acquired skill (malaka) that had to be learned, so that it became one of the crafts and trades, as will be mentioned in the chapter on knowledge and teaching. The people of group solidarity were busy with upholding royal authority and sovereignty, so the task of knowledge was handed over to those among others who took it up, and it became a trade for livelihood. The noses of the pampered and the people of sovereignty were raised too high to undertake teaching; taking it up became confined to the weak, and whoever took it up came to be despised among the people of group solidarity and royal authority. And as for al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, his father was one of the chiefs of Thaqīf and their nobles, and their place in the group solidarity of the Arabs and in rivaling Quraysh in nobility is what you know

and his teaching of the Qurʾān was not as the matter stands in the present age, a trade for livelihood; it was, rather, as we have described of the first order in Islam. Of this kind also is what those who skim through history books imagine when they hear of the circumstances of the judges and the leadership they held in wars and the command of armies: the whisperings of ambition fling them toward such ranks, and they reckon that the office of judge in the present age is as it was before. When they hear that the fathers of Ibn Abī ʿĀmir, Hishām’s associate who seized sole control over him, and of Ibn ʿAbbād, one of the Party Kings in Seville, were judges, they suppose that they were like the judges of the present age, not noticing the change in customs that has come about in the rank of judge, as we shall explain in the chapter on the judiciary in Book One. Ibn Abī ʿĀmir and Ibn ʿAbbād were of the Arab tribes that upheld the Umayyad dynasty in al-Andalus, people of its group solidarity, and their position in it was well known; they did not attain what they attained of leadership and royal authority through the office of judge as it is in the present age. Rather, in the old order the judgeship went to people of group solidarity from the dynasty’s own kin and its clients, just as the vizierate does in our time in the Maghrib

Consider their going out with armies in the Party Kingdoms and their being entrusted with great matters that are entrusted only to someone who has the capacity for them through group solidarity. The hearer errs in this and takes the circumstances to be other than they are. Those who most often fall into this error are those weak in insight among the people of al-Andalus in the present age, because group solidarity has been lacking in their homelands for long ages, owing to the extinction of the Arabs and their dynasty there and their passing out of the dominion of the people of the group solidarities among the Berbers. Their Arab lineages have remained preserved, but the means to might through group solidarity and mutual support is missing; they have become, rather, among the subjects who fail one another, whom coercion has enslaved and who have grown used to humiliation. They suppose that their lineages, together with mixing with the dynasty, are what will give them mastery and authority; so you find the people of trades and crafts among them setting themselves to this and striving to attain it. But as for those who have dealt at first hand with the conditions of the tribes and group solidarity and their dynasties on the western shore, and with how domination comes about among nations and clans, they seldom err in this and seldom go wrong in assessing it.

Of this kind also is what historians do when they mention dynasties and the sequence of their kings: they mention his name, his lineage, his father, his mother, his wives, his title, his signet, his judge, his chamberlain and his vizier, all in imitation of the historians of the two dynasties, without noticing their aims. The historians of that age wrote their histories for the people of the dynasty, whose sons were eager for the lives of their ancestors and a knowledge of their circumstances, so as to follow in their traces and weave on their loom, even in taking men into patronage from among those who came after in their dynasty, and in assigning offices and ranks to the sons of their protégés and kin. The judges too were of the dynasty’s people of group solidarity and ranked among the viziers, as we have told you, so they needed to mention all of that. But when dynasties became separate and the distance between ages grew, and the purpose came to be limited to knowing the kings themselves in particular, and how dynasties compare with one another in strength and victory, and which nations rivaled them or fell short of them, what benefit is there for the author in the present age in mentioning sons, wives, the engraving of the signet, the title, the judge, the vizier and the chamberlain of an ancient dynasty in which their origins, lineages and stations are not known? What drove them to it was only imitation, heedlessness of the aims of the earlier authors and obliviousness to pursuing the purposes of history. The exception is the viziers whose achievements were great and whose reports have effaced those of the kings, such as al-Ḥajjāj, the Banū al-Muhallab, the Barmakids, the Banū Sahl ibn Nawbakht, Kāfūr al-Ikhshīdī, Ibn Abī ʿĀmir and the like: there is nothing objectionable in alluding to their fathers and indicating their circumstances, since they ranked among the kings.

Let us mention here a benefit with which we close our discussion in this section: history is only the recording of the reports particular to an age or a generation; as for the recording of the general conditions of the regions, generations and ages, it is a foundation for the historian, on which most of his aims are built and by which his reports are made clear. People used to devote separate works to it, as al-Masʿūdī did in his book Murūj al-dhahab (“The Meadows of Gold”), in which he explained the conditions of the nations and regions of his time, in the period of the year 330, in the west and the east; he mentioned their creeds and customs, described the lands, mountains, seas, kingdoms and dynasties, and the divisions of the peoples of the Arabs and the non-Arabs; so he became an imam for the historians, to whom they refer, and a source on which they rely in verifying many of their reports. Then al-Bakrī came after him and did likewise for routes and realms in particular, to the exclusion of other conditions, because the nations and generations of his time had not undergone much movement or great change. But in the present age, the end of the eighth century, the conditions of the Maghrib, which we have witnessed, have been overturned and changed altogether: it has taken in exchange for the generations of the Berbers, its people from of old, the generations of the Arabs who have come into it since the fifth century, for they broke them, overcame them, took most of their homelands from them and shared with them what remained of the lands in their possession; this, in addition to what befell civilization in the East

and the West, in the middle of this eighth century, from the sweeping plague that wore down the nations, carried off the people of a generation, and swept away and effaced many of civilization’s fair features. It came upon the dynasties at the time of their senility and their reaching the limit of their span; it shrank their shade, blunted their edge and weakened their sovereignty, and their wealth crumbled into dissolution and vanishing. The civilization of the earth was undone with the undoing of mankind: cities and buildings fell into ruin, roads and landmarks were effaced, dwellings and abodes were emptied, dynasties and tribes weakened, and the inhabitants changed. It is as if I see the East afflicted with the like of what afflicted the Maghrib, but in proportion to it and to the extent of its civilization. It was as though the tongue of existence called out to the world to sink into obscurity and contraction, and the world hastened to answer; and God is the inheritor of the earth and all upon it. When conditions change altogether, it is as though creation were changed from its very root and the whole world transformed, as though it were a new creation, a renewed genesis, a newly originated world. So in this age there is need of someone who will record the conditions of creation and of the regions and their generations, and the customs and creeds that have changed for their people, and who will follow al-Masʿūdī’s course for his own time, so as to be a basis that the historians who come after him can follow. In this book of mine I shall record, as far as I am able, what I can of this in this Maghribī region, either explicitly or contained within its reports, or by allusion, since my aim in composition is directed especially to the Maghrib and the conditions of its generations and nations and the mention of its kingdoms and dynasties, to the exclusion of other regions, because I have no acquaintance with the conditions of the East and its nations

and because transmitted reports do not suffice for the true nature of what I want from it. Al-Masʿūdī covered it fully only because of the length of his journeying and his moving about the lands, as he mentions in his book, although when he mentioned the Maghrib he fell short in covering its conditions. And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows. All knowledge returns to God; man is incapable and deficient, and confession of this is required and obligatory. Whoever has God as his helper finds the ways made easy for him, and his endeavors and requests meet with success. We are setting out, with God’s help, on the purposes of composition that we have aimed at; God is the one who guides aright and helps, and upon Him is reliance. It remains for us to set forth a preliminary note on how to write the letters that do not belong to the languages of the Arabs, when they occur in this book of ours.

Know that letters in speech, as the explanation will come later, are the modes of the sounds that issue from the larynx; they arise from the breaking up of the sound by the striking of the uvula and the tips of the tongue against the palate, the throat and the molars, or by the striking of the lips as well. The modes of sounds differ with the difference of that striking, and the letters come out distinct to the ear, and out of them are composed the words that indicate what is in the mind. Nations are not all alike in pronouncing these letters: one nation may have letters that another lacks. The letters that the Arabs pronounce are twenty-eight, as you know. We find that the Hebrews have letters that are not in our language, and our language has letters that are not in theirs; the same is true of the Franks, the Turks, the Berbers and other non-Arabs. Then the scribes among the Arabs agreed to signify their audible letters by the forms of written letters, distinguished by their individual shapes, such as the setting down of alif, bāʾ, jīm, rāʾ and ṭāʾ, up to the last of the twenty-eight. When a letter occurs to them that is not among the letters of their language, it remains neglected as regards written indication and left unmarked in the exposition. Some scribes sometimes write it in the shape of the letter of our language that flanks it, before or after; but that is not enough to indicate it; it is rather a change of the letter at its very root.

Since our book comprises reports on the Berbers and some non-Arabs, and in their names or some of their words there occur letters that do not belong to the language of our writing or the convention of our letter-forms, we were obliged to make it clear. We were not content with writing the letter that flanks it, as we said, because in our view that is insufficient to indicate it. So in this book of mine I have adopted the convention of writing that non-Arabic letter with signs that indicate the two letters flanking it, so that the reader, in pronouncing it, takes a middle course between the points of articulation of those two letters, and its rendering is achieved. I took this only from the practice of the copyists of the Qurʾān codices in writing the letters of ishmām, as in al-ṣirāṭ in Khalaf’s reading: the pronunciation of its ṣād there is modified, intermediate between ṣād and zāy, so they put the ṣād and draw inside it the shape of the zāy, and that signifies for them the intermediate position between the two letters. In the same way I write every letter that is intermediate between two of our letters, such as the kāf that is intermediate among the Berbers between our pure kāf and the jīm or qāf, as in the name Bulukkīn: I write it as a kāf and dot it with the dot of the jīm, a single one below, or with the dot of the qāf, a single one above or two, and that indicates that it is intermediate between the kāf and the jīm or qāf. This letter occurs most often in the Berber language, and as for what occurs of any other,

then, on this analogy, I write the letter that is intermediate between two letters of our language with both letters together, so that the reader knows that it is intermediate and pronounces it accordingly; thus we have indicated it. Had we written it in the form of the single letter beside it, we would have turned it from its point of articulation to that of the letter that belongs to our language, and altered the language of the people. Know this, then; and God is the One who grants success in what is right, by His favor and bounty.
